headings.title: Introduction to Electronic Health Records
headings.content: An **Electronic Health Record (EHR)** is a digital version of a patient's paper chart that tracks medical history, treatments, and vital signs in real time. In Nigerian healthcare facilities, transitioning from paper records to digital systems helps reduce medication errors and missing charts. An EHR allows authorized clinicians across different departments to access up-to-date patient information instantly. This shared visibility supports faster clinical decision-making during emergencies.

headings.title: Acute Care versus Ambulatory EHR Systems
headings.content:
- **Acute Care EHR**: Built for hospitals and emergency units where patients stay overnight. It focuses on rapid vital sign charting, inpatient medication administration, and surgical scheduling.
- **Ambulatory EHR**: Designed for outpatient clinics, general practices, and community health centers. It emphasizes long-term wellness tracking, scheduled appointments, and chronic disease management.

headings.title: Specialty-Specific and Enterprise EHR Solutions
headings.content: Large teaching hospitals often use **Enterprise EHR Systems** that connect every department—from pharmacy to laboratory and maternity—into one central database. This prevents data silos within massive medical complexes. Meanwhile, specialized clinics like pediatrics, obstetrics, or eye clinics require **Specialty-Specific EHRs** featuring tailored templates. A pediatric chart, for example, prioritizes growth curves and immunization schedules over adult chronic illness tracking.

headings.title: Personal Health Records and Patient Portals
headings.content: Patient portals and **Personal Health Records (PHRs)** shift some control into the hands of the patient. A patient portal is securely linked to the hospital's EHR, allowing patients to view lab results or book clinic visits. A PHR, however, is managed entirely by the patient, who inputs their own blood pressure readings, diet history, and drug allergies. Nurses often teach patients how to navigate these tools to improve self-management of chronic illnesses like hypertension.

headings.title: Cloud-Based versus On-Premise EHR Infrastructure
headings.content:
| Feature | Cloud-Based EHR | On-Premise EHR |
|---|---|---| 
| **Data Storage** | Remote secure servers accessed via internet | Local physical servers inside the hospital |
| **Upfront Cost** | Lower subscription model | High hardware and installation cost |
| **Maintenance** | Managed by the vendor | Managed by internal IT staff |

In settings with unstable electricity or internet connectivity, such as rural Nigerian primary health centers, on-premise or hybrid models are often preferred to prevent downtime during patient care.

headings.title: Implications for Nursing Practice and Patient Safety
headings.content: The type of EHR directly impacts daily nursing workflows and patient safety. Systems with built-in barcode medication administration (BCMA) help nurses verify the five rights of drug administration at the bedside. However, poorly designed interfaces can cause **alert fatigue**, where nurses ignore repetitive pop-up warnings. Understanding different EHR platforms ensures nurses can document accurately while keeping patient care safe and efficient.
